theory.intro: Rectangles with the same area can have different side lengths, and rectangles with the same perimeter can also have different shapes.
facts: Area $=$ length $\times$ width; many length/width pairs give the **same area**.
Perimeter $=$ $2 \times (\text{length} + \text{width})$; many pairs give the **same perimeter**.
Same area does **not** mean same perimeter, and the reverse is also true.
steps: List length/width pairs that multiply to the target area (or add to half the perimeter).
Compute the other measure (perimeter or area) for each pair.
Compare to see how the shape changes.

foundation.question_text: A rectangle has area $24\text{ cm}^{2}$ and length $8$ cm. Find its width.
List all different rectangles with whole-number side lengths and area $18\text{ cm}^{2}$. Treat a rotation as the same rectangle.
foundation.solution_text:
$1\times18=18$
$2\times9=18$
$3\times6=18$
The dimensions are $1$ cm by $18$ cm, $2$ cm by $9$ cm, and $3$ cm by $6$ cm.

foundation.question_text: List all different rectangles with whole-number side lengths and perimeter $16$ cm. Treat a rotation as the same rectangle.
foundation.solution_text:
$l+w=16\div2$
$=8$
The pairs that add to $8$ are $(1,7)$, $(2,6)$, $(3,5)$ and $(4,4)$.
The dimensions are $1$ cm by $7$ cm, $2$ cm by $6$ cm, $3$ cm by $5$ cm, and $4$ cm by $4$ cm.

foundation.question_text: Two rectangles have the same area. Must they have the same perimeter? Use the $3$ cm by $8$ cm and $4$ cm by $6$ cm rectangles to decide.
foundation.solution_text:
$3\times8=24\text{ cm}^{2}$ and $4\times6=24\text{ cm}^{2}$
$2(3+8)=22\text{ cm}$
$2(4+6)=20\text{ cm}$
They have the same area but different perimeters, so they do not have to share a perimeter.

development.question_text:
Complete the table of whole-number dimensions for rectangles of area $36\text{ m}^{2}$.
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Length (m)}&\text{Width (m)}\\\hline1&36\\2&18\\3&12\\4&\square\\6&6\end{array}$
Rectangles A and B both have area $48\text{ cm}^{2}$. A is $12$ cm by $4$ cm. B is $8$ cm long. Find B's width, then decide which rectangle has the smaller perimeter.
development.solution_text:
$8\times w=48$
$w=6\text{ cm}$
$P_A=2(12+4)$
$=32\text{ cm}$
$P_B=2(8+6)$
$=28\text{ cm}$
Rectangle B has the smaller perimeter.

development.question_text: Two rectangular display boards each have perimeter $28$ m. One is $11$ m by $3$ m and the other is $8$ m by $6$ m. Compare their areas.
development.solution_text:
$A_{11\times3}=11\times3$
$=33\text{ m}^{2}$
$A_{8\times6}=8\times6$
$=48\text{ m}^{2}$
The $8$ m by $6$ m board has $15\text{ m}^{2}$ more area.

development.question_text: All whole-number rectangles with perimeter $24$ cm have side lengths that add to $12$ cm. List the possible dimension pairs and identify the one with the greatest area.
development.solution_text:
The pairs are $(1,11)$, $(2,10)$, $(3,9)$, $(4,8)$, $(5,7)$ and $(6,6)$.
Their areas are $11$, $20$, $27$, $32$, $35$ and $36\text{ cm}^{2}$.
The $6$ cm by $6$ cm rectangle has the greatest area, $36\text{ cm}^{2}$.

development.question_text: All whole-number rectangles with area $40\text{ cm}^{2}$ are listed by factor pairs. Complete the list and identify which has the least perimeter: $(1,40)$, $(2,20)$, $(4,10)$, $(\square,\square)$.
development.solution_text:
$5\times8=40$
The missing pair is $(5,8)$.
The perimeters are $82$, $44$, $28$ and $26$ cm.
The $5$ cm by $8$ cm rectangle has the least perimeter.

development.question_text: A rectangle is changed from $10$ cm by $4$ cm to $8$ cm by $5$ cm. Describe what stays the same and what changes.
development.solution_text:
$10\times4=40\text{ cm}^{2}$ and $8\times5=40\text{ cm}^{2}$, so the area stays the same.
$2(10+4)=28\text{ cm}$ and $2(8+5)=26\text{ cm}$, so the perimeter decreases by $2$ cm.

mastery.question_text: A rectangle has whole-number side lengths, area $60\text{ cm}^{2}$ and perimeter $34$ cm. Find its dimensions.
mastery.solution_text:
Factor pairs of $60$ are $(1,60)$, $(2,30)$, $(3,20)$, $(4,15)$, $(5,12)$ and $(6,10)$.
A perimeter of $34$ cm means $l+w=17$ cm.
$5+12=17$
The dimensions are $5$ cm by $12$ cm.

mastery.question_text: A whole-number rectangle has perimeter $30$ cm. Find all possible dimension pairs, then determine the greatest possible area.
Sofia claims that among whole-number rectangles with the same area, the rectangle whose side lengths are closest together has the smallest perimeter. Test her claim for area $72\text{ cm}^{2}$.
mastery.solution_text:
The factor pairs are $(1,72)$, $(2,36)$, $(3,24)$, $(4,18)$, $(6,12)$ and $(8,9)$.
Their perimeters are $146$, $76$, $54$, $44$, $36$ and $34$ cm.
The closest pair is $8$ and $9$, and it gives the smallest perimeter, $34$ cm.
Sofia's claim is true for area $72\text{ cm}^{2}$.
